metadata.title: What We Chased Before.
metadata.clock: narration (Kokoro af_bella) - per-beat mp3 durations are MEASURED, never estimated
metadata.greeting_note: hello lexicon. SKILL.md limits the HAI persona to the SHORTEST forms only - Hi / Ola / Hej / Ciao. All four are used, so from Ep. 09 the lexicon CYCLES least-recently-used first: Hej (03), Ciao (04), Ola (05), Hi (08), Hej (09). Least recently used is now Ciao, last seen at Ep. 04.
metadata.target_runtime: Under 3:00 BY DESIGN. 423 words against Ep. 09's measured 0.3752 s/word predicts 2:38.7, leaving ~21 s of margin. The words-only model is noise of order +-5-10% with NO consistent sign - Ep. 06 +10.4%, Ep. 07 -0.4%, Ep. 08 -5.0%, Ep. 09 +2.7% - so the margin is for noise, not for a predicted direction.
metadata.purpose: Ep. 10 of the AI in Astronomy & Space Science series, from weekly_stem_videos/ideas.md Astronomy topic 10 (Classifying supernovae in real time - AI triaging which transient sky events astronomers should chase before they fade).
metadata.color_semantics: Claude fidelity palette. Terracotta #D97757 is the ONE accent and marks WHAT DOUBT FINDS - the rare class in every plot, the uncertainty-sampling picks, the exploration quota, the recall curve that actually moves. Ink marks THE CONFIDENT MAJORITY - the well-sampled classes, the accuracy number that rises while nothing improves, the count of confirmed Ia that exploration costs you. The mapping never flips, so B06 teaches it once and every later plate reads for free. Accented text is #A44A32; #B9B4A0 is strokes and fills only.
metadata.distinct_from_earlier_episodes: Eps. 01-06 had AI inspecting observations; Ep. 07 standing in for a calculation; Ep. 08 a division of labour; Ep. 09 an output that was never a measurement. Ep. 10 is the first episode where the TRAINING SET ITSELF is the output of the system's own past decisions, through a scarce resource and human hands. The limit is therefore new - not an accuracy ceiling (Ep. 04), an unseen class (Ep. 03), an irreversible rejection (Ep. 05), a latency (Ep. 06), a circularity through simulation (Ep. 07), a misreading (Ep. 08) or non-identifiability (Ep. 09), but a CLOSED FEEDBACK LOOP: what got followed up became what got labelled, which became what the model can recognise, which decides what gets followed up next.
metadata.note: ILLUSTRATE LAW: the Claude UI appears at B00, B11, B12, B13. Every other beat illustrates its concept as a reel-local Manim scene (scenes.py). All plates come from assets/gen_triage.py, which RUNS a real closed-loop experiment: 60 repeats x 12 seasons x 20 spectra, three follow-up strategies, a hand-written Gaussian naive Bayes chosen precisely BECAUSE a class with no labels cannot be predicted, so the feedback mechanism is visible in the model rather than buried in an ensemble. The central claim is ASSERTED and the script writes nothing if it fails. Results are reported as MEDIANS, because the outcome is bimodal and a 12-repeat mean read 0.088 where the median is 0.000. PUBLISHED numbers and COMPUTED-HERE numbers are kept apart on screen and in the narration. No published figure is reproduced or redrawn. No LaTeX/MathTex anywhere. metadata.channel_title is omitted for the GATE V edge-bleed reason logged in Ep. 03. scenes.py is ASPECT-AWARE: one file lays out 16:9 and the 9:16 derivative.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Om Mali. This video is about how AI decides which exploding stars are worth pointing a telescope at tonight, and why the ones it skips are the ones nobody ever finds.

show.event: cream page; IRREDUCIBLY HUMAN eyebrow, then the serif segment title
spark + greeting Ciao, HAI settles above the composer card
the ask types itself into the composer; send button arms when it lands
terracotta running indicator: ranking tonight's 200,000 alerts...
three result lines stagger in - pressure, loop, fix. The ask lands ANSWERED.

props.command: Telescopes find far more exploding stars than anyone can follow up. How does a model decide which ones to chase, what does that decision do to the next model, and what would fix it?
output: pressure - a transient fades in days; about one in ten ever gets a spectrum
loop - the training set IS the record of past choices, so the model repeats them
fix - spend part of the budget where the model is least sure, not most

beats.narration_text: Nine episodes of AI looking at the sky. This one is about AI deciding what we look at next.

show.event: OM MALI writes in, terracotta hairline underlines it
role line fades in beneath: Humanitarians AI - presenter
a card draws beside it
row one lands and is STRUCK: nine episodes / AI looks at the sky
row two lands in the accent and is boxed: this one / AI chooses what we look at
closer: Ep. 10 - the sample is the decision

beats.narration_text: A supernova fades in days. There are far more of them than there are telescopes, so something has to choose. And the thing doing the choosing learned from what we chose last time.

show.event: a card lands, empty
kinetic set one: IT FADES IN DAYS / decide tonight
set two: THERE ARE TOO MANY / something must choose
set three lands in the accent and is underlined: IT LEARNED FROM OUR LAST CHOICE
closer: the loop was already closed

beats.narration_text: A transient peaks and fades within about two weeks, so a spectrum is only useful early. Rubin will report up to ten million changes a night. About one in ten ever gets one.

show.event: three computed light curves rise and fall on one set of axes
a shaded band lands over the first twelve days: the useful window
a terracotta rule drops at the window's edge
a counter: up to 10,000,000 alerts a night
a second, much smaller counter beside it: about 1 in 10 gets a spectrum
closer: the decision cannot wait

beats.narration_text: And which ones? The bright ones. Almost every transient brighter than magnitude eighteen gets confirmed. Down at twenty and fainter, closer to one in seven. Nobody wrote that rule down.

show.event: four bars draw, one per brightness band
the two bright bars fill almost to the top in ink
the two faint bars fill barely at all; their empty part rings terracotta
a label under the axis: peak magnitude
a quiet line: published confirmation fractions, not measured here
closer: nobody wrote that rule down

beats.narration_text: So the labelled set is not a sample of the sky. It is a record of what we chased. Train on it and you get a model that is best at exactly the things we already looked at.

show.event: four boxes draw in a ring: WE CHOOSE / IT GETS A LABEL / THE MODEL LEARNS IT / IT RECOMMENDS MORE
a terracotta arc closes the ring, arrowhead landing back on the first box
the ring pulses once
a chip lands: the training set is the output of the last decision
closer: best at what we already looked at

beats.narration_text: I ran that loop. Twelve seasons, twenty spectra each, spent where the model is most confident. Accuracy climbs. The rare class? In forty-eight runs out of sixty it is never recognised once.

show.event: two empty panels draw side by side, labelled accuracy and rare-class recall
in the left panel three curves climb; they all rise
in the right panel the terracotta curve climbs while two ink curves stay flat on the axis
the flat pair is ringed
a counter lands in the accent: 48 of 60 runs, never once
closer: accuracy never warned anyone

beats.narration_text: You can see why. After two hundred and forty spectra, the rare class is two tenths of one percent of everything labelled. The loop kept confirming what it already knew.

show.event: two stacked-bar panels draw, season by season
the left panel's terracotta sliver stays invisible across twelve seasons
the right panel's terracotta band grows season on season
two figures land beneath: 0.19% and 16.8%
closer: it kept confirming what it knew

beats.narration_text: Now change one thing. Spend the budget where the model is least sure, nearest the line it cannot draw. That is a real deployed rule. And doubt moves - toward the thing nobody has labelled.

show.event: a feature-space panel lands: the population as faint dots
the labelled seed lights in ink, all clustered in one place
terracotta rings mark where the next spectra go - along the boundary
a second panel replaces it: eight seasons later, the rings have migrated
two figures land: 3.6x the base rate, then 8.4x
closer: doubt goes where the labels are not

beats.narration_text: In a real run on a real telescope, that strategy reached the same performance with a quarter fewer spectra, and turned up microlensing and flaring stars that were never in anyone's training set.

show.event: a card heads DEPLOYED, NOT SIMULATED
row one: 92 spectra against 127, for the same performance
a terracotta chip: 25% fewer
row two types in: microlensing · flaring stars
a struck line beneath them: not in the training set
closer: it found things nobody asked for

beats.narration_text: So the tell. A classifier trained on past choices repeats them, and accuracy never warns you. Spend one night in ten on what you do not understand: a third becomes nine in ten.

show.event: a card heads WHAT THE ACCURACY NUMBER HIDES
row one lands in ink and is STRUCK: the model is getting better
row two lands in the accent and is boxed: the model is getting narrower
beside it the trade-off curve draws: exploration against the chance of ever finding the rare class
a marker drops at ten percent; two figures land: 35% becomes 92%
a quiet ink line: and costs 18% of the confirmations
closer: one night in ten

beats.narration_text: So: the sample is the decision. Confidence buys more of what you have. Doubt is the only thing that buys something new, and it costs less than you would think.

show.event: the artefact page opens on the cream stage
line one lands
line two lands
line three lands
line four lands in the accent

props.artifactTitle: What We Chased Before - one page
artifactLines: A transient fades in days, and only about one in ten ever gets a spectrum.
Which ones? Historically the bright ones - so the labelled set records our choices, not the sky.
Train on that and spend the budget on confidence, and the rare class is never recognised at all.
Spend one night in ten where the model is least sure, and a third becomes nine in ten.
It costs about 18% of the confirmed Ia. That is the whole price.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Read it: my model was trained on data that earlier decisions produced. Help me work out what it can never learn, and the cheapest experiment that would show me. Run it on a model you rely on.

show.event: the composer returns, greeting fixed to Your turn.
the prompt types itself in as it is read aloud
terracotta running indicator: paste this into Claude...
three grading lines stagger in as the rubric is spoken

props.command: My model was trained on data that earlier decisions produced. Help me work out what it can never learn from that data, and design the cheapest experiment that would show me.
output: grade it: does it ask HOW THE DATA WAS COLLECTED, not just what is in it
grade it: does it name a class the data CANNOT contain
grade it: does the experiment cost less than the status quo

a terracotta rule, then the handle
the series subline settles
